catalog_quote: In terms of word prosody, Sgaw Karen does not exhibit word stress cues, but does maintain a prosodic distinction between the more prominent major syllable and the phonologically reduced minor syllable. [p. ii] ... In short, contrary to the stress correlates found in some tonal languages, intensity and duration in Sgaw Karen are not found to correlate to syllable position consistently. Moreover, duration and intensity patterns do not seem linked to the age or sex of the speaker. This section has presented the finding that neither intensity nor duration consistently distinguish major syllables within a word, suggesting that word-level stress is not a feature of Sgaw Karen. [p. 24] ... new_statements.quote: Minor syllable are always stressless and never bear a distinct tone. Minor syllables are composed of an initial C and mid central vowel /ə/. The initial consonant of a minor syllable is generally a stop. Minor syllables are phonologically bound to a following major syllable. (Lar 2001, p27) [p. 99] ... Lar (2001) states that "all major syllables include a tone" (p27) [p. 98] ... Consonants which appear alone without any vowel signs or tone marks are unaccented syllables which are linguistically connected to the following syllable. They have a neutral vowel sound like the sound of the "a" in "about," and the tone is usually somewhere around mid tone. (Ballard 1993, p42) [p. 99] ... No coda is present, and the T is any of the six aforementioned tones. [p. 102]

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Sgaw Karen has an empty rule. This work adds: tonal (six tones on every major syllable), no word-stress rule stated, minor presyllables stressless and toneless (quoted from Lar 2001). Nothing to contradict.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Sgaw Karen is a tone language: every major syllable carries one of six tones (in the consultant's dialect). The only stress-related statement is second-hand, quoted from Lar (2001) and Ballard (1993): minor (reduced /ə/) presyllables are 'always stressless' / 'unaccented' and toneless and are bound to the following major syllable, so prominence within a sesquisyllabic word lies on the tone-bearing major syllable. No word-stress placement rule is given for polysyllabic words; Fischer herself takes no position on the phonological status of minor syllables (she suggests the /ə/ may be epenthetic) and calls for further research.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the author says the criteria for minor syllables and their phonetic properties (duration, tone) remain to be established (p. 101).
new_statements.identity_note: Fischer 2013 describes the idiolect of one consultant, Ms. Tri Sa ('TS'), who grew up in Myeik (Mergui), Burma, lived 28 years in Mae Sot, Thailand, and then in Chapel Hill-Carrboro, North Carolina; the thesis compares her six-tone system with Moulmein and Bassein Sgaw (Jones 1961) and Yangon Sgaw (Lar 2001). Sarvestani 2018 describes the variety spoken in the Sgaw Karen refugee community of Buffalo, New York, and relates it to previously published varieties. Both are Sgaw Karen proper (sgaw1245), diaspora varieties.

new_statements.quote: Minor syllables lack codas and (in languages with weight distinctions) should be phonologically light. Minor syllables should lack stress and, in tonal languages, contrastive tones (Michaud, 2012). [p. 70] ... The status of these syllables is difficult to determine due to disagreement among linguists about what constitutes a minor syllable. Additionally, Sgaw phonology is not suited to making a well-motivated determination: the lack codas or obvious evidence of syllable weight or stress and the phonemic status of /ə/ complicate the matter. Finally, and importantly, if these syllables do constitute minor syllables in Sgaw, then they should lack tonal contrasts, putting them beyond the central focus of this dissertation. [pp. 70-71]

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog rule is empty; this work supplies the explicit statement that there is no obvious evidence of word stress or syllable weight in Sgaw, and that the language is tonal. Compatible with Fischer 2013.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Sgaw Karen (Buffalo refugee-community variety) is a tone language with a 'Southeast Asian type of tone system' on a largely monosyllabic or sesquisyllabic lexicon; the dissertation states that Sgaw shows no obvious evidence of syllable weight or stress (and no codas), and remains agnostic on whether the reduced-/ə/ presyllables are true minor syllables. No word-stress placement is described.
new_statements.identity_note: Fischer 2013 describes the idiolect of one consultant, Ms. Tri Sa ('TS'), who grew up in Myeik (Mergui), Burma, lived 28 years in Mae Sot, Thailand, and then in Chapel Hill-Carrboro, North Carolina; the thesis compares her six-tone system with Moulmein and Bassein Sgaw (Jones 1961) and Yangon Sgaw (Lar 2001). Sarvestani 2018 describes the variety spoken in the Sgaw Karen refugee community of Buffalo, New York, and relates it to previously published varieties. Both are Sgaw Karen proper (sgaw1245), diaspora varieties.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: every segment of the deciding quotation, and the the secondary-stress rule fragments, are verbatim in the West 2017 text we hold at the stated pages (ii, 24, 32-33); Gilmore 1898 sec. 14-15 (six tones) also. (2) The classification 'no-word-stress' (not in the strict set) rests on a 2017 instrumental MA thesis whose explicit research question is Sgaw word stress, supervised by Sun-Ah Jun; among Glottolog's 25 descriptive refs the grammars are 1842-1961 missionary/structuralist works and the phonologies are Puttachart 1983 (124 pp MA), Sarvestani 2018 (183 pp PhD) and Fischer 2013 (sketch). None of these is known to contain a stress experiment; West's own literature review says prior descriptions have 'little to no description of word prosody'.
